title: Shia communities today
hook: in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, India and beyond

segments.voice: Yesterday, traditional Sufi orders today, and your line: the orders today. A circle before dawn, a wird, a teacher. Did you give one repeated morning thing your full attention? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

A small disc of baked clay, about the size of a coin, sits on a prayer mat. When the person praying bows down, the forehead touches the clay. You'll find discs like that in homes in Baghdad and Beirut, in Baku and Manama, in Karachi and Lucknow, in Detroit and London. It's one quiet sign of a Shia household, among others. The communities around it speak Arabic, Persian, Azerbaijani, Urdu, English. They live in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, India and beyond. Today, a short tour of where they are and what holds them together.
screen: `A DISC OF CLAY ON THE MAT.` → `BAGHDAD, BAKU, KARACHI, DETROIT.` → `WHAT HOLDS THEM TOGETHER?`

segments.voice: First, the center. Shia is short for shi'at Ali, a phrase Shia Muslims explain as the followers of Ali. Shia Muslims hold that after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, leadership belonged to his household, beginning with Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, and passing through a line of Imams. They point, among other texts, to a hadith that Sunni collections keep too. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people: the Book of Allah, and his household, whom he asks them to remember. Second, the family within. The Twelvers, named for the line of Imams they recognize, are one branch. Zaydis, found especially in Yemen, and Isma'ilis, tomorrow's lesson, are other branches with their own histories. Third, the places that hold a community. In Iraq, Lebanon and Bahrain there is the husayniyya, a hall for gathering and mourning Husayn. In Pakistan and India the same kind of hall is called an imambargah. There are seminaries in Najaf and Qom, where students train for years. And Twelvers follow a living senior scholar, a marja', on questions of law, so a believer in Chicago may follow a scholar in Najaf. Fourth, the shared floor. Shia and Sunni Muslims pray toward the same Ka'bah, fast the same Ramadan, go on the same Hajj and read the same Qur'an. Shia often join the noon prayer with the afternoon, and the sunset prayer with the night, and pray on that clay disc, which they explain as bowing onto earth, not onto a carpet. Different customs, the same direction.
screen: `SHI'AT ALI: THE FOLLOWERS OF ALI.` · `TWELVERS, ZAYDIS, ISMA'ILIS.` · `HUSAYNIYYA, IMAMBARGAH, SEMINARY.` · `THE SAME KA'BAH, THE SAME QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about one community. Start in the sit. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the clay disc on the mat, and the cities from the hook. Choose one of them: Beirut, Baku, Manama, Lucknow, or a Shia center in your own city. For a few breaths, simply hold that place in mind: people waking up there, praying there, going to work there. If you pray, you can ask for good for them in your own words. Later, read about that one community from its own members: its mosque, its hall, its customs. The bell holds the time.
Shia communities today. Muslims who follow the household of the Prophet through Ali and the Imams, living from Iran and Iraq to Pakistan, India and beyond. Today's word.

Your line: shia around the world. Today, find one of the countries from today's list on a map, and read one paragraph about the Shia community that lives there. Tomorrow, the Isma'ilis. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Shia Muslims pray toward the Ka'bah like other Muslims, often joining the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers, and placing the forehead on a small clay tablet; they gather in mosques and in halls called husayniyyas or imambargahs, and Twelvers follow a living senior scholar, a marja', on questions of law.

No count of Imams and no size claims are given; Twelvers are described only as named for their line of Imams.
The clay disc (turbah or mohr) and the joining of prayers should be checked by a Shia scholar for fair description.
